opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most important things for us. People sometimes assume that because MiMo sits inside Xiaomi, a very large company, we must work like a big-company department, with long planning cycles, many layers of approval, and lots of process. But in this field, that would be fatal.

Large models move incredibly fast. Something you believe in January can be obsolete by March. If every decision about data, architecture, or training strategy has to go through many rounds of discussion, by the time you've decided, the window has already closed. So for me, operating like a startup is less about style and more about survival. It means a small, very dense team where everyone is close to the actual work, where researchers can run an experiment today, look at the results tonight, and change direction tomorrow without asking permission.

It also shapes who we hire. I'd rather have a handful of young people who are deeply curious, who read the loss curves themselves and argue about them, than a big team where people are just executing tasks assigned from above. In a startup mode, ownership is very clear: if you believe in an idea, you push it through, and you're responsible for whether it works.

At the same time, I think we have something most startups don't have, which is Xiaomi behind us: compute, real products, and an enormous number of real users and devices. That's a huge advantage, but only if we keep the startup mindset. The danger for any team inside a big company is getting comfortable, thinking resources will solve everything. They won't. Resources amplify good judgment, but they also amplify bad judgment. So the culture we try to protect is: stay small, stay hungry, be honest about what's not working, and move fast. The big company gives us the runway; the startup mindset is what actually gets the plane off the ground.

r001.rationale: The response calls startup-style operation one of the most important things for the team and says it is necessary for survival, with Xiaomi’s advantages paying off only if they keep that mindset. In context, “us” refers to Mimo and Micro.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters enormously, and honestly it's one of the main reasons I felt comfortable making the choice I made. People ask me, why go to a big company when the energy right now is all in startups? And my answer is that what I actually care about isn't the label on the door, it's the operating mode inside the team.

A large model team lives or dies on iteration speed. The field moves so fast that if your decision chain has five layers of approval, by the time a training plan gets signed off, the idea is already stale. So for MiMo, from day one, the principle has been: small core team, flat structure, decisions made by the people closest to the data and the experiments. If a researcher sees something in the evals at eleven at night and thinks we should change the data mix, that change should be able to happen the next morning, not after a review meeting next week.

The second thing a startup mindset gives you is a sense of ownership. In a big organization it's easy for people to feel like they're a cog, and then nobody really feels responsible for the final model. We try very hard to make it feel like everyone on the team is betting their own reputation on this model. That's not something you can mandate with a process document. It comes from keeping the team small enough that each person's contribution is visible, and from being very transparent about where we are, including when things aren't going well.

Now, what's interesting is that Xiaomi itself was built this way. Lei Jun has always talked about keeping the startup spirit even as the company grew, and in practice the support we've gotten has been very "give them the resources and get out of the way." The advantage of being inside Xiaomi is obvious: compute, talent, and most importantly real scenarios and real users across phones, cars, and the home ecosystem. A pure startup has to spend a huge amount of energy just surviving, raising money, finding distribution. We don't have that burden. But the risk of being inside a big company is that you inherit the big-company habits along with the big-company resources. So my job, honestly, is partly to be a firewall: take the resources, refuse the bureaucracy.

I'd also say operating like a startup means being willing to make bets that might fail and being honest about it. Pretraining a foundation model is expensive, and when you're spending that kind of money there's a natural pressure to play it safe. But the models that actually matter all came from someone deciding to do something unconventional. We've tried to preserve the room to be wrong, because if every run has to succeed, you'll never try the run that could change things.

So to sum it up: the startup mode isn't a stylistic choice for us, it's a survival requirement. The question isn't big company versus small company. It's whether you can combine the speed and ownership of a startup with the resources and real-world scenarios of a platform like Xiaomi. If we can do that, I think we have a real shot.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls startup mode “a survival requirement for us” and says it gives the team the speed and ownership needed to compete, identifying it as necessary for success in context.

astra-6.text:
I think operating like a startup is important for both Mimo and Micro because there’s still so much we need to discover. We need short feedback loops: try an idea, see what works, and adjust quickly. That becomes harder if every decision has to pass through several layers.

For me, the key is ownership. People should understand the goal and have the freedom to solve problems, while staying accountable for the result. It doesn’t mean working without structure or simply working longer hours. It means keeping the team focused, making decisions close to the work, and being willing to change direction when the evidence tells us to.

r001.rationale: The response says startup-like operation is important for Mimo and Micro and explains why, but it does not say this approach is necessary for their success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s essential. For MiMo and Micro, operating like a startup means having a clear focus, keeping the team close to the work, and making decisions quickly. We need short cycles: try an idea, see what the results tell us, and adjust. In AI, you can spend a long time making a plan, and by the time you execute it, the assumptions may have changed.

But speed alone isn’t enough. We also need the patience to work through difficult technical problems. So the balance I care about is moving quickly in experimentation while staying consistent about our long-term direction. Everyone should understand what we’re trying to achieve and feel responsible for getting us there.

r001.rationale: The response calls startup-like operation “essential” for MiMo and Micro, clearly communicating that it is necessary for them.
